title: Web app on Kubernetes
summary: A load balancer spreads requests over app pods on Kubernetes, which check Redis before going to PostgreSQL.
intro: The workhorse shape for a web product that outgrew one server. Your app is packaged as a container image and runs as several identical pods on Kubernetes, which restarts them when they crash and adds more when they’re busy. A load balancer spreads traffic across them. Frequently read data is answered from a Redis cache, so PostgreSQL only handles the misses and the writes.
fits: Product teams with steady traffic and several services

diagram.caption: Requests are spread across the pods. Each pod asks Redis first; hits come straight back, misses go on to PostgreSQL. Every 12 seconds one pod is taken down and the load balancer routes around it while Kubernetes replaces it.

steps.title: The load balancer picks a healthy pod
steps.text: An Application Load Balancer receives each request and forwards it to one of the pods registered as healthy. A pod that fails two health checks in a row (sent every 30 seconds by default) stops getting traffic.

steps.title: Kubernetes keeps the pods running
steps.text: A Deployment asks for three replicas of the `api` image. If one crashes or its node dies, Kubernetes starts a replacement; a HorizontalPodAutoscaler can add replicas when CPU climbs.

steps.title: Redis answers the common reads
steps.text: The app looks up the key in Redis first. On a hit it returns immediately; on a miss it queries PostgreSQL and stores the result in Redis with an expiry, so the next request is a hit.

steps.title: PostgreSQL holds the truth
steps.text: All writes and cache misses go to PostgreSQL. It’s the one stateful piece, so it usually runs as a managed service with a standby replica and automatic backups.

good: Pods are interchangeable, so losing one costs nothing but a little capacity
The cache takes most of the read load off the database, which is the hardest part to scale
The same container image runs in development, CI and production
Kubernetes gives one way to deploy, scale and roll back every service the team runs
watch: Kubernetes itself is a system to learn, upgrade and secure; managed offerings help but don’t remove that
Cache invalidation: after a write, stale entries must be deleted or allowed to expire
PostgreSQL is still one primary; heavy write growth eventually needs read replicas, partitioning or sharding
If Redis goes down, every request becomes a miss; make sure the database can survive that surge

swaps.text: Not ready for Kubernetes? Run the same containers on Fargate or Cloud Run and let the platform manage the machines.
Self-hosted or multi-cloud? Use NGINX as an ingress in front of the pods instead of a cloud load balancer.
Add Prometheus to scrape every pod and Grafana to chart it, so you see the cache hit rate and database latency.
Deploy with Argo CD: it watches a Git repository and keeps the cluster matching it.
